Article.ArticleTitle: Open-source, high-speed and high-resolution data acquisition platform for biopotential recordings and neural EIT applications.

Abstract.AbstractText: Objective.Biopotential measurement devices, such as electroencephalography, electrocardiography (ECG), and electromyography (EMG) recorders, are available in low-cost, open-source implementations with standard specifications. However, high-end systems remain expensive and predominantly proprietary, limiting accessibility and customization by research laboratories. In addition, neurophysiology techniques such as bioimpedance-based fast neural electrical impedance tomography (FN-EIT) also rely on these systems for data acquisition. This work aimed to develop an open-source biopotential recording system using off-the-shelf components that achieves performance comparable to high-end devices.Approach.We designed our system to provide simultaneous sampling over 32 channels, 24-bit resolution, 10 kHz bandwidth, 50 kHz sampling rate, and battery-powered operation while reducing cost by two orders of magnitude. System performance was evaluated comparatively against a reference device. Initial validation involved benchtop recordings in saline solution and standard non-invasive biopotential measurements (ECG and EMG). Furtherin-vivovalidation was performed by recording evoked electrophysiological responses and FN-EIT traces from the sciatic nerve of a rat during tibial branch stimulation.Main results.EMG recordings showed comparable RMS peak amplitudes (814 ± 153µV vs 897 ± 113µV,p= 0.07), while ECG-derived heart rates closely matched between systems (64.8 ± 4.0 bpm vs 65.1 ± 3.1 bpm,p= 0.54). Duringin-vivorecordings, compound action potentials exhibited comparable amplitudes and morphology (129 ± 26 mV vs 128 ± 25 mV,P= 0.15). FN-EIT recordings showed strongly correlated baseline voltages (R> 0.93,P= 0.11), sub-microvolt noise levels (0.83 ± 0.36µV vs 0.42 ± 0.25µV,p< 0.05), and comparable impedance variations (0.006 ± 0.002% vs 0.005 ± 0.003,P> 0.05). FN-EIT images of functional activity recorded with the novel device closely matched reference ones, exhibiting a 98.5% overlap in activated area.Significance.The proposed open-source device has the potential to broaden research access to customizable, high-specification data acquisition hardware and facilitate wider adoption of specialized neural recording techniques such as FN-EIT.

Article.ArticleTitle: Rapid-Onset Subacute Combined Degeneration After Short-Term, High-Dose Nitrous Oxide Use.

Abstract.AbstractText: Recreational nitrous oxide (N2O) use has risen in recent years and is increasingly accessible in high-volume cartridges and canisters. N2O oxidizes cobalamin and functionally inhibits methionine synthase disrupting methylation pathways essential for myelin maintenance and DNA metabolism. Serum vitamin B12 levels may be normal despite functional deficiency, making markers such as homocysteine and methylmalonic acid helpful to confirm the diagnosis. Clinical manifestations range from peripheral neuropathy and megaloblastic anemia to subacute combined degeneration (SCD), a demyelinating myelopathy classically involving the dorsal columns (and sometimes corticospinal tracts). Although SCD is often associated with chronic exposure, brief but high-dose use may precipitate rapid neurologic decline. Early recognition and prompt parenteral vitamin B12 replacement may reduce the risk of irreversible deficits.

Article.ArticleTitle: Pearls & Oy-sters: Beyond the Bone Marrow-VEXAS Syndrome Presenting as Subacute Encephalomyelitis.

Abstract.AbstractText: Vacuoles, E1 enzyme, X-linked, Autoinflammatory, Somatic (VEXAS) syndrome is an adult-onset autoinflammatory disease caused by acquired somatic UBA1 mutations, typically presenting with systemic inflammation and myelodysplastic syndrome. Although infrequent, neurologic manifestations can include peripheral neuropathy, stroke, or encephalopathy. Notably, spinal cord involvement remains poorly documented. Here, we present the case of a 70-year-old man with myelodysplastic syndrome and confirmed VEXAS (UBA1 p.Met41Thr) presenting with subacute ascending paresthesia, Lhermitte sign, and urinary hesitancy suggestive of myelopathy. 3T MRI demonstrated multifocal T2-hyperintense spinal cord and brain lesions, some with contrast enhancement, consistent with inflammatory encephalomyelitis. CSF analysis showed mild lymphocytic pleocytosis (33 cells/µL), elevated protein (55 mg/dL), and numerous CSF-restricted oligoclonal bands. Negative infectious PCR testing and the absence of aquaporin 4 and myelin oligodendrocyte glycoprotein antibodies argued against infection or other inflammatory demyelinating condition. The patient received high-dose intravenous methylprednisolone (1 g/d for 3 days), resulting in rapid clinical improvement. Follow-up MRI performed 1 month after presentation showed resolution of contrast enhancement and partial disappearance of spinal T2 hyperintense lesions.

Article.ArticleTitle: Role of the SGK1/GSK-3β/β-Catenin Signaling Pathway in Thalamic Hemorrhage-Induced Central Post-Stroke Pain in Mice.

Abstract.AbstractText: Central post-stroke pain (CPSP) is a chronic neuropathic pain condition associated with thalamic injury and frequently accompanied by affective disturbances. Although SGK1 has been implicated in neuroinflammation and behavioral regulation, its role and underlying mechanisms in CPSP remain unclear. In this study, a thalamic hemorrhage mouse model was established by collagenase injection to investigate the contribution of SGK1 to CPSP-like phenotypes. Behavioral assessments were performed to evaluate pain hypersensitivity, cold allodynia, and anxiety-like behaviors. Pharmacological inhibition and viral-mediated overexpression of SGK1 were used to examine its effects on pathological injury, inflammatory responses, and the GSK-3β/β-catenin signaling pathway. Thalamic hemorrhage induced persistent mechanical allodynia, cold hypersensitivity, and anxiety-like behaviors. SGK1 expression was upregulated in microglia and astrocytes, peaked at day 7, and remained elevated until day 28 after hemorrhage. SGK1 inhibition alleviated pain-related behaviors, pathological damage, and neuroinflammation, whereas SGK1 overexpression produced opposite effects. Mechanistically, SGK1 modulation was associated with changes in GSK-3β Ser9 phosphorylation, β-catenin accumulation, and inflammatory cytokine expression. These findings identify SGK1 as a critical regulator of CPSP progression and suggest that targeting the SGK1/GSK-3β/β-catenin signaling axis may represent a potential therapeutic strategy for post-stroke pain.

Article.ArticleTitle: The Effect of Bupropion in Peripheral Neuropathic Pain A Randomized, Double-Blind, Placebo-Controlled Study.

Abstract.AbstractText: Monoamine reuptake inhibitors are evidenced first-line treatments of peripheral neuropathic pain. The aim was to investigate if bupropion, a drug that specifically inhibits neuronal noradrenaline and dopamine reuptake, relieves neuropathic pain and if a potential effect depends on status of conditioned pain modulation (CPM) and sensory phenotype (irritable vs. non-irritable nociceptor).

Study design was randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled, and cross-over. Patients with peripheral neuropathic pain were treated with bupropion and placebo in a random order, with treatment periods lasting 6 weeks preceded by a 1-week baseline. Change in daily average pain was the primary outcome. Other outcomes included pain relief and 30% and 50% pain reduction.

67 patients were randomized and included in the analysis. The mean daily average pain changed from NRS 6.4 to 5.5 after bupropion treatment with an average effect as compared with placebo of -0.5 (95% CI -0.8 to -0.1, p = 0.005). No relation was found between response to treatment and efficiency of CPM or sensory phenotype. There was no significant effect on the pain relief scale. A 30% and 50% pain reduction was found in 10 and 6 patients respectively with a NNT for 50% pain reduction of 15. Bupropion was well tolerated.

Bupropion had a pain-relieving effect independent of CPM efficiency and sensory phenotype. NNT for 50% pain reduction was higher than reported for first-line treatments, but bupropion treatment may still be an option in patients with insufficient response or intolerable side effects on such treatments.

This study finds a modest pain-relieving effect of bupropion on peripheral neuropathic pain independent of function of conditioned pain modulation. Bupropion could be an alternative treatment for patients with a lack of effect or intolerable side effects to first-choice treatments of peripheral neuropathic pain. Further, larger studies are needed to determine optimal dosage.

The study is registered with the EU clinical trials Register (EudraCT 2019-000243-27) on March 15th 2019. The study is approved by the Ethical Committee of the Region of Southern Denmark (also included approval for Regions of Central Denmark; no. S-20190010) and the Danish Medicine Agency (no. 2019012986) and is registered with the Danish Data Protection Agency (via the Region of Southern Denmark's internal notification; no. 19/17111).

Article.ArticleTitle: Long-term analgesic use after neuroma and upper limb nerve injury: patterns in Sweden.

Abstract.AbstractText: To examine demographic and socioeconomic differences in diagnosis and treatment of neuroma and nerve injury, assess risk of long-term use of centrally acting analgesics (CA-analgesics) compared with the general population, and describe how long-term use is distributed among individuals by demographic, socioeconomic, and treatment characteristics.

In linked Swedish national registers (5,625,751 individuals, 25-80 years, residing 2010), incident cases of nonsurgically or surgically treated neuromas (n = 608' n = 189, respectively) or nerve injuries (n = 3,719, n = 2,122, respectively) were identified (no clinical data available) 2011 to 2014 and long-term CA-analgesic use was defined (prescription coverage ≥60% of days during 1 year; 60-day washout period after surgery). Multinomial and binary logistic regression models were used to estimate relative risks, adjusted for sex, age, income level, country of birth, and cohabiting. Absolute risks and absolute risk differences were calculated.

Neuroma or nerve injury cases were identified with variation in diagnosis and treatment by demographic and socioeconomic factors; women more likely to undergo neuroma surgery; men and younger individuals predominated among nerve injuries. All diagnostic treatment groups had markedly increased risks of long-term CA-analgesic use compared with the general population (adjusted relative risk range 3.5-6.0). Absolute risks among individuals exceeded 10% in socioeconomically disadvantaged subgroups (approximately 0.5% in the general population). Differences in long-term CA-analgesic use between nonsurgically and surgically treated individuals were modest.

Neuroma and nerve injuries are associated with a substantial risk of long-term CA-analgesic use. Socioeconomic disadvantage strongly influences risk, whereas surgical treatment does not consistently reduce long-term medication use.

Article.ArticleTitle: Combined Nav1.7-Nav1.8 channel abrogation: Supralinear suppression of excitability in a subpopulation of peripheral sensory neurons.

Abstract.AbstractText: There is a pressing need for nonaddictive pain therapeutics. Despite the genetic validation of peripheral voltage-gated sodium (Nav) channels as targets for non-opioid pain therapy, isoform-selective inhibition of Nav1.7 and Nav1.8 has yielded limited efficacy in clinical studies, with Nav1.8 blockade providing statistically significant but only partial pain relief. This raises the question: if block of Nav1.8 relieves pain only partially, what is needed for better pain relief? In this study, we utilized dynamic clamp, which permits precisely calibrated functional addition or subtraction of the current from any given channel, to systematically interrogate the combinatorial landscape of multiplex abrogation of currents from Nav1.7 and Nav1.8, both major contributors to electrogenesis within dorsal root ganglion neurons. We demonstrate that partial, simultaneous attenuation of both conductances drives a supralinear increase in current threshold in many sensory neurons. Responses to Nav1.8 functional subtraction span a broad spectrum, whereas responses to Nav1.7 subtraction are comparatively uniform. Neurons with greater sensitivity to functional loss of Nav1.8 show greater suppression of excitability during combined Nav1.7-Nav1.8 attenuation, while weak Nav1.8 responders remain comparatively resistant. These findings identify electrogenic dependence on Nav1.8 as a major source of functional heterogeneity in sensory neurons and demonstrate that Nav1.7 acts cooperatively with Nav1.8 to shape the consequences of channel attenuation. Our results indicate that combined Nav1.7-Nav1.8 targeting should outperform isoform-selective block in suppressing firing in a subpopulation of pain-signaling neurons, while not producing universal suppression.

Article.ArticleTitle: The Effect of Implementing Orem's Self-Care Model on Balance and Fatigue in Patients With Diabetic Neuropathy: A Clinical Trial.

Abstract.AbstractText: This study aims to determine the effect of applying Orem's self-care model on balance and fatigue in patients with diabetic neuropathy.
Randomized clinical trial.

Seventy diabetic neuropathy patients referred to Shahid Mofateh Clinic, affiliated with Yasuj University of Medical Sciences (YUMS), were chosen for this clinical trial study via convenience sampling and randomly assigned to an intervention group (n = 35) or a control group (n = 35). The intervention group received care based on Orem's self-care model from a graduate nursing student over 2 months, followed by 1 month of self-care at home. The control group received no intervention. Both groups completed the research questionnaires (the Multidimensional Fatigue Inventory and the Berg Balance Test) at pretest and posttest. Data were analysed in SPSS version 27 using an ANCOVA test.

Before the intervention, there were no significant between-group differences (p > 0.05). After the intervention, fatigue was significantly lower in the intervention group, with an adjusted mean difference of -9.40 points (95% CI: -11.09 to -7.71; p < 0.001; partial η2 = 0.647). Balance scores were significantly higher in the intervention group across low, mean, and high baseline levels, with adjusted mean differences of 7.01, 5.77, and 4.52 points, respectively (all p < 0.001). The group × baseline balance interaction was significant (F(1,66) = 5.69, p = 0.020; partial η2 = 0.079).
Nurses are recommended to apply Orem's self-care model as an effective structured intervention to reduce fatigue and improve balance in patients with diabetic neuropathy.

Patients with diabetic peripheral neuropathy (diagnosed by an internist using TCSS) who participated in this randomized clinical trial evaluating Orem's self-care model effects on balance and fatigue.

Article.ArticleTitle: Baseline Peripheral Neuropathy Predicts Clinically Significant Neuropathy During Paclitaxel Treatment Following Oxaliplatin-based Chemotherapy.

Abstract.AbstractText: Chemotherapy-induced peripheral neuropathy (CIPN) is a common dose-limiting toxicity that adversely affects quality of life and treatment continuity of patients with malignancy. Although cumulative oxaliplatin exposure is a recognized risk factor for neurotoxicity, it remains unclear whether cumulative exposure or baseline neurological status better predicts clinically significant CIPN during subsequent paclitaxel treatment. This study aimed to identify predictors of clinically significant CIPN during paclitaxel therapy, focusing on the relative predictive value of cumulative oxaliplatin exposure and baseline CIPN.

We retrospectively reviewed 76 patients with advanced gastric cancer who received paclitaxel-based second-line therapy after oxaliplatin-containing first-line chemotherapy. The primary endpoint was time to development of grade ≥2 CIPN, and the secondary endpoint was CIPN worsening. Cox proportional hazards and multivariable logistic regression analyses were performed to identify factors associated with CIPN progression.

Grade ≥2 CIPN developed in 34 patients (44.7%). Baseline CIPN (grade 1 vs. 0) independently predicted subsequent grade ≥2 CIPN (hazard ratio=4.23, 95% confidence interval=1.67-10.72; p=0.002; odds ratio=5.00, 95% confidence interval=1.58-15.80; p=0.006). In contrast, cumulative oxaliplatin dose was not associated with grade ≥2 CIPN or CIPN worsening. Kaplan-Meier analysis also showed no association between cumulative oxaliplatin dose and time to CIPN worsening, whereas higher serum albumin levels tended to be associated with a lower risk of CIPN progression.

Baseline CIPN was a stronger predictor of clinically significant neuropathy during paclitaxel treatment than prior cumulative oxaliplatin exposure. Routine assessment of baseline neurological status before paclitaxel initiation may help identify patients at high risk for clinically significant CIPN and support individualized treatment and monitoring strategies.

Article.ArticleTitle: Aligned PCL conduits integrated with tranilast-loaded GelMA hydrogel for immune-regulated peripheral nerve regeneration.

Abstract.AbstractText: Effective peripheral nerve repair requires coordinated topographical guidance, remyelination, and immune microenvironment remodeling within nerve guidance conduits. However, conventional conduits often provide passive bridging with limited inflammatory regulation. Here, we developed a tranilast-loaded gelatin methacryloyl (GelMA) hydrogel-filled aligned polycaprolactone (PCL) conduit (H-TG) by integrating high-speed-collected electrospun PCL fibers with a locally immunomodulatory hydrogel. The aligned PCL conduit provided ordered physical cues that enhanced neuronal-like PC12 cell responses and rat Schwann cell (RSC) adhesion, spreading, and regeneration-associated marker expression in vitro. Meanwhile, under H2O2 exposure, tranilast reduced CD86 and iNOS expression and increased Arg1 and CD206 expression, indicating a shift toward a reparative macrophage-associated phenotype. In a rat 10 mm sciatic nerve defect model, H-TG promoted functional recovery, axonal regeneration, and remyelination, reduced the g-ratio, attenuated gastrocnemius muscle atrophy, and improved nerve histomorphology. Furthermore, H-TG decreased CD68+iNOS+ M1-like macrophages and TNF-α expression while increasing CD68+CD206+ M2-like macrophages and IL-10 expression. These findings support an aligned and immunomodulatory conduit strategy for peripheral nerve regeneration.

Article.ArticleTitle: Spontaneous neuropathic pain.

Abstract.AbstractText: Spontaneous pain is a highly prevalent and disabling consequence of neuropathic disorders, yet it remains mechanistically underdefined and therapeutically underserved. Historically, preclinical animal models and clinical trials have been overwhelmingly biased toward stimulus-evoked hypersensitivity, relegating spontaneous pain to a secondary manifestation. Emerging evidence now challenges this view. Converging data from pharmacology, neural recordings, and systems-level causal manipulations indicate that spontaneous and stimulus-evoked pain arise from substantially dissociable molecular, cellular, and circuit substrates. Injured-fiber-derived ectopic activity within specific sensory neuron subtypes serves as a dominant peripheral generator of spontaneous pain, whereas cellularly distinct, intact spared-fiber pathways mediate stimulus-evoked hypersensitivity. At spinal and supraspinal levels, spontaneous pain preferentially engages affective-salience networks during pain chronification and may ultimately become stabilized within higher-order circuitry-while remaining dynamically coupled to afferent input. This mechanistic delineation carries critical translational implications. Current diagnostic and treatment guidelines rarely differentiate symptom domains, and most therapies have been validated primarily using stimulus-evoked or overall pain intensity endpoints-potentially contributing to a mechanism-therapy mismatch and variable efficacy. We argue that spontaneous neuropathic pain should be defined as a separate symptom domain rather than considered as a spontaneous manifestation of evoked pain mechanisms. This recognition demands longitudinal, biomarker-informed phenotyping to capture its persistent and fluctuating nature, and thereby enable robust mechanistic dissection at peripheral, spinal, and cortical nodes. Reframing spontaneous neuropathic pain along these lines will provide a foundation for precision therapeutics that target defined cell types, specific molecular drivers, and maladaptive network states-enabling mechanism-based, symptom-aligned treatments.

Article.ArticleTitle: An integrative view of human nociceptor diversity: from microneurography to molecular identity.

Abstract.AbstractText: Neuropathic pain arises from dysfunction of the peripheral or central nervous system and affects up to 10% of the population worldwide. Aberrant activity in injured sensory nerve fibers, particularly spontaneous firing and altered conduction properties of nociceptors, is tightly linked to pain, yet its molecular underpinnings in humans have long remained elusive. Over recent years, major technological advances have transformed both functional and molecular analyses of sensory neurons. High-resolution single-cell and spatial transcriptomics have produced detailed atlases of sensory neuron diversity, while traditional electrophysiological approaches such as patch-clamp and microneurography have provided unparalleled insight into nerve fiber properties. Despite their individual strengths, molecular and functional classifications of sensory neurons have largely evolved in parallel. This review focuses on emerging strategies that bridge these approaches to achieve an integrated, mechanistic understanding of neuropathic pain. We discuss how microneurography-defined biophysical hallmarks, such as activity-dependent slowing, recovery cycle signatures, and following frequency, can be transferred into in vitro patch-clamp paradigms, enabling direct functional comparison with dissociated human and large-animal sensory neurons. The incorporation of Patch-seq approaches has further enabled the assignment of molecular identity to functionally defined nociceptor subtypes, exemplified by the characterization of the mechano-insensitive "sleeping" nociceptors. Finally, we highlight how multimodal datasets combining electrophysiology, transcriptomics, and computational modeling provide new opportunities to unravel the ion channel mechanisms, particularly sodium channel subtypes, that shape pathological firing states. By directly linking human nerve fiber function to molecular programs, this integrative framework paves the way toward stratified, mechanism-based therapies for neuropathic pain.

Article.ArticleTitle: The neuropathic chameleon: we are hot on the scent.

Abstract.AbstractText: A common chronic pain condition, neuropathic pain arises from a lesion or disease affecting the somatosensory or neural tissue and is characterized by a combination of negative (eg, numbness) and positive (eg, burning pain) sensory symptoms that significantly affect the quality of life. Common comorbidities such as depression and sleep disruption contribute to a substantial disease burden, which is further exacerbated by the apparent lack of effective therapeutic options. Current treatment options frequently achieve only partial, insufficient pain relief or may be completely ineffective in a considerable number of patients. The development of new drugs has thus far achieved moderate success, with many clinical trials failing to meet their primary endpoints; thus, a substantial unmet clinical need persists. One reason for this therapeutic deadlock is the considerable heterogeneity of neuropathic pain, driven by diverse pathophysiological mechanisms that vary between patients regardless of the underlying disease etiology. Accordingly, reclassification efforts follow a mechanism-based approach that reflects pathophysiological pain generators rather than disease etiology. Although diagnosis remains anchored in lesion- or disease-based criteria and structured clinical assessment, treatment development increasingly benefits from mechanism-informed phenotyping. A priori stratification based on individual mechanisms may help identify treatment responders, but implementation requires surrogate markers, as no biomarkers for pain mechanisms currently exist. In this article, we discuss candidate predictive markers and surrogate markers, focusing on sensory symptoms and signs assessed through patient-reported outcome measures and sensory testing, and their integration into future clinical trials.

Article.ArticleTitle: Molecular histochemical analysis of neuroplasticity-related gene expression in pain pathway.

Abstract.AbstractText: I am deeply honored to receive the 2026 John Bonica Prize for distinguished lifetime achievement in the basic science of pain. Reflecting on 40 years of research, this review paper will summarize my key findings to date. For the past four decades, my research has focused on elucidating the molecular mechanisms of pain using animal models. By integrating morphological techniques with molecular biology, behavioral analysis, and electrophysiological recordings, I have sought to clarify how pain signals are modulated and sustained under chronic pain conditions. Since the early stages of my career, I have been particularly interested in the diverse molecular dynamics within pain pathways and their functional significance. This long-term research has been driven by the conviction that a detailed analysis of gene expression changes within pain pathways-particularly those associated with neuroplasticity-is essential to understanding the mechanisms underlying intractable pain. This review provides a comprehensive overview of our investigation into the molecular and cellular mechanisms of chronic pain, focusing on gene expression analyses related mainly to dorsal root ganglion and spinal cord plasticity, alongside historically significant contributions from the global pain research community. Finally, I will also discuss recent methodological advances and their applications, as well as the challenges and future directions facing basic pain research.

Article.ArticleTitle: Under pressure: lessons from and beyond entrapment neuropathies.

Abstract.AbstractText: Entrapment neuropathies are the most prevalent focal neuropathic pain conditions globally and impose a substantial individual and socioeconomic burden. Traditionally conceptualised as purely mechanical compression syndromes, this view is increasingly challenged by converging evidence from human tissue analyses, advanced neuroimaging, and deep clinical phenotyping. Entrapment neuropathies are now recognised as biologically dynamic disorders shaped to different extents by microvascular compromise, demyelination, axonal degeneration, immune dysregulation, neuroinflammation, central nervous system adaptations, and psychosocial influences. Varying combinations and dominance of biopsychosocial processes give rise to marked clinical heterogeneity even within the same diagnostic label. This mechanistic diversity helps explain common diagnostic discordances, including extraterritorial symptom spread, normal electrodiagnostic findings despite clinical symptoms indicative of entrapment neuropathies, and imaging-clinical presentation mismatch. It also challenges one-size-fits-all treatment approaches, which have largely failed in entrapment neuropathies.Uniquely, entrapment neuropathies provide a natural human model of focal nerve injury in the context of neuropathic pain. Surgical decompression allows integration of tissue-level biology with precise clinical phenotypes and offers time-locked insights into recovery. Lessons derived from this model extend beyond entrapment neuropathies and can inform broader understanding of neuropathic and nerve-related musculoskeletal pain conditions. Here, we synthesise contemporary mechanistic insights, examine how biological heterogeneity translates into distinct clinical phenotypes, and discuss potential implications for mechanism-informed management.

Article.ArticleTitle: Peripheral neuroimmune dialogues underlying pain states.

Abstract.AbstractText: Pain is profoundly shaped by neuroimmune interactions within peripheral tissues. Nociceptors are specialized sensory neurons that express receptors for cytokines, lipid mediators, complement components, antibodies and microbial signals, enabling immune mediators to directly modulate neuronal excitability. In turn, nociceptors influence immune cell and stromal cell activity through the release of neuropeptides and cytokines. Some of these pathways are shared across multiple tissues in pathological pain states, whereas others reflect the distinct immune and stromal environments of the skin, joints, muscles, gut, peripheral nerves, sensory ganglia and meninges. Across these sites, immune-to-neuron signalling orchestrates the initiation and amplification of pain, while maladaptive feedback loops reinforce hypersensitivity. In concert, coordinated neuroimmune signalling also contributes to pain resolution by restoring homeostasis. Emerging human studies reveal convergent neuroimmune signatures across nociceptive, neuropathic and nociplastic pain conditions, underscoring their translational relevance. By integrating both shared mechanisms and tissue-specific mechanisms, this Review highlights how peripheral neuroimmune crosstalk shapes pain across diverse contexts. Furthermore, it outlines therapeutic opportunities to rebalance these pathways, offering prospects for durable and mechanism-based analgesia.

Article.ArticleTitle: [Chronic pain after dental implant placement in the interforaminal region].

Abstract.AbstractText: Neuropathic pain following implant placement is a rare but taxing outcome of an otherwise generally safe procedure. This case report describes a 37-year-old patient who presented with persistent pain after placement of implants in the interforaminal region. Radiographic imaging revealed that the apex of the implants was very close to the mandibular incisive canal, possibly explaining the neuropathic pain. Diagnostic local anesthesia relieved the pain completely. On the basis of this outcome, the implants were removed, after which the complaints disappeared. After a period of three months without pain, renewed implant placement was considered and it was decided to place two new implants. The patient remained pain-free after implantation and a new overdenture could be made, with which the patient functioned well. This case emphasizes the importance of early recognition of neuropathic pain following implant placement, and shared decision making with the patient in determining treatment strategy and managing expectations regarding its outcomes.

Article.VernacularTitle: Chronische pijn na plaatsen van implantaten in interforaminale regio.

OtherAbstract.AbstractText: Neuropathische pijn na implantaatplaatsing is een zeldzame maar belastende complicatie van een doorgaans veilige ingreep. Deze casus beschrijft een 37-jarige pati nt met persisterende pijnklachten na plaatsing van implantaten in de interforaminale regio. Radiologische beeldvorming toonde dat de apex van de implantaten zich in nauwe relatie tot de canalis incisivus mandibulae bevond, wat een mogelijke verklaring vormde voor de neuropathische pijn. Diagnostische proefanesthesie resulteerde in volledige pijnreductie. Op basis hiervan werden de implantaten verwijderd, waarna de klachten verdwenen. Na een pijnvrije periode van drie maanden werd herimplantatie overwogen en werd besloten twee nieuwe implantaten te plaatsen. Postoperatief bleef de pati nt klachtenvrij en kon een nieuwe overkappingsprothese worden vervaardigd, waarmee zij goed functioneert. Deze casus benadrukt het belang van vroege herkenning van neuropathische pijn na implantaatplaatsing en van gedeelde besluitvorming met een pati nt bij het bepalen van de behandelstrategie en het managen van verwachtingen omtrent behandeluitkomsten.

Article.ArticleTitle: Biomechanical Evolution in the Neuropathic Diabetic Foot: A Scoping Review of Gait and Kinetic-Kinematic-Structural Adaptations in Diabetes.

Abstract.AbstractText: Gait alterations and biomechanical changes associated with diabetic peripheral polyneuropathy have been described in the literature, but the available evidence remains fragmented. It does not provide a comprehensive overview of how the reported biomechanical patterns differ across clinical stages of the Neuropathic Diabetic Foot (NDF). Mapping these patterns may support an improved understanding of the biomechanical mechanisms underlying increased ulceration risk.

This scoping review aims to explore and synthesise the existing literature on changes in gait and foot biomechanics in people with diabetes in association with Diabetic Peripheral Neuropathy (DPN) and across its reported clinical stages.

The scoping review was conducted in accordance with the JBI methodology for scoping reviews and in line with the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses extension for Scoping Reviews (PRISMA-ScR). The population included adults with diabetes and peripheral neuropathy, without active foot ulceration, who were managed in community or outpatient settings. The concept of interest is gait and foot-biomechanical alterations associated with diabetic neuropathy in clinical and biomechanical assessment contexts. A comprehensive search was conducted in PubMed, EMBASE, CINAHL, PEDro, and the Cochrane Library, complemented by grey literature sources including the Trip Medical Database, NICE, and the Guidelines International Network (GIN). Studies published within the last 11 years were considered (2014/12-2026/04). Data were charted and synthesised using a descriptive and narrative approach.

From 2044 initial records, 44 sources met the eligibility criteria. An updated search conducted in April 2026 identified 6 additional eligible sources, resulting in 50 included sources. The evidence mapped across three principal themes: gait and lower-limb kinematic alterations, changes in plantar loading and joint kinetics, and structural or functional changes of the foot. No included study directly evaluated whether the identified biomechanical alterations predicted the subsequent development of Charcot neuro-osteoarthropathy.

To our knowledge, this is the first scoping review to map structural, kinematic, kinetic, and plantar-loading findings within an integrated biomechanical framework of the neuropathic diabetic foot. Because the evidence was predominantly cross-sectional, the proposed relationships should be interpreted as a conceptual synthesis rather than a demonstrated longitudinal progression. These findings highlight the need for longitudinal studies to investigate the temporal evolution of biomechanical alterations in the neuropathic diabetic foot.

Article.ArticleTitle: Zdhhc14 promotes pyroptosis in the dorsal root ganglion of oxaliplatin-induced peripheral neuropathy mice by enhancing GBP5 palmitoylation and suppressing its ubiquitination.

Abstract.AbstractText: Oxaliplatin-related neuropathy (OIPN) remains a frequent chemotherapy-induced complication, yet its underlying mechanisms remain incompletely understood. Emerging evidence implicates pyroptosis in OIPN pathogenesis, and palmitoylation has been recognised as a critical mechanism in neurological disorders.
This investigation set out to examine the part played by the palmitoyltransferase Zdhhc14 in pyroptosis in OIPN as well as to clarify the fundamental molecular processes.

A mouse model of OIPN was developed through intraperitoneal oxaliplatin administration, and primary neuronal cultures derived from dorsal root ganglia were exposed to oxaliplatin to simulate OIPN in vitro. Bioinformatics analysis was performed using the GSE255097 dataset. Gene and protein expression were examined by quantitative real-time PCR, Western blot and immunofluorescence staining. Pyroptosis was assessed by lactate dehydrogenase release, flow cytometry and detection of pyroptosis-related proteins. Co-immunoprecipitation, immunoprecipitation and cycloheximide chase assay were applied to evaluate the mechanisms.

Zdhhc14 was significantly up-regulated in dorsal root ganglion (DRG) of OIPN mice in a time-dependent manner. Zdhhc14 deficiency alleviated OIPN phenotypes, including mechanical hyperalgesia and cold allodynia, neuroinflammation and DRG pyroptosis. Mechanistically, Zdhhc14 binds to GBP5 and promotes its modification at Cys12, which is required for Zdhhc14-mediated suppression of K48-linked ubiquitination and subsequent proteasomal degradation, thereby stabilising GBP5. GBP5 knockdown phenocopied the protective effects of Zdhhc14 deficiency, whereas GBP5 overexpression reversed these effects. Importantly, mutation of the GBP5 palmitoylation site abolished the pro-pyroptotic effects of Zdhhc14.

These findings indicate that the Zdhhc14/GBP5 palmitoylation axis critically regulates DRG pyroptosis and neuroinflammation in OIPN, identifying a novel mechanism and a potential mechanistic target warranting further translational evaluation for this debilitating condition.

Article.ArticleTitle: Adolescent-onset spastic paraplegia associated with a TUBB4A p.Gly96Arg variant: insights from diffusion tensor tractography.

Abstract.AbstractText: Adolescent-onset spastic paraplegia may present with heterogeneous underlying pathophysiology, including both axonal and myelin-related mechanisms. We report a 53-year-old woman with progressive spastic paraplegia beginning in adolescence who was found to harbor a pathogenic TUBB4A p.Gly96Arg variant. Brain magnetic resonance imaging showed diffuse white-matter abnormalities and thinning of the corpus callosum, without basal ganglia or cerebellar atrophy, mimicking hereditary spastic paraplegia. Compared with three older healthy controls, diffusion tensor imaging (DTI)-based tractography showed lower fractional anisotropy and higher apparent diffusion coefficient across the corpus callosum, corticospinal tract, and middle cerebellar peduncle. Mean tract length was shorter in the corpus callosum but near the control means in the corticospinal tract and middle cerebellar peduncle, while streamline-count deviations also varied by tract. In this genetically confirmed case, DTI-based tractography provided supportive, hypothesis-generating characterization of white matter microstructural involvement. However, these observations do not establish an underlying pathological mechanism or an independent differential diagnostic role for DTI.

Article.ArticleTitle: A disynaptic trigeminal circuit for the transformation and integration of oral chemesthesis in male mice.

Abstract.AbstractText: Chemesthesis, encompassing oral sensations such as spiciness and coolness, is an important yet incompletely understood component of mammalian chemical sensing. Unlike taste or olfaction, these sensations are conveyed primarily through trigeminal pathways; however, how modality-specific peripheral signals are processed and transformed along central ascending pathways remains poorly understood. Herein, we delineate the structural and functional organization of an ascending trigeminal-brainstem-parabrachial circuit that mediates oral chemesthetic processing in male mice. Using viral tracing, in vivo calcium imaging, and chemogenetic and optogenetic manipulations, we identify a genetically defined disynaptic glutamatergic pathway (trigeminal ganglion → spinal trigeminal nucleus caudalis → lateral parabrachial nucleus) that is both necessary and sufficient for capsaicin- and menthol-evoked defensive behaviors. Although peripheral TRPV1+ and TRPM8+ neurons retain a degree of modality bias, we observe substantial convergence of spicy and cooling signals within the spinal trigeminal nucleus, followed by sustained and synchronized population activity in vglut2+ neurons of the external lateral parabrachial nucleus. This hierarchical transformation from peripheral segregation to central integration reveals the organizational principle by which distinct chemesthetic modalities are progressively integrated along a trigeminal-mediated ascending pathway, providing a circuit-level framework for understanding how chemical stimuli are processed and coordinated to drive defensive behaviors.

Journal.Title: International journal of psychiatry in medicine

Article.ArticleTitle: SSRIs and SNRIs in Hematology - A Systematic Review and Qualitative Analysis.

Abstract.AbstractText: BackgroundDepression and neurotoxic complications are frequently observed in patients with hematologic malignancies (HM). Serotonergic antidepressants, mainly selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) and serotonine-norepinephrine reuptake inhibitors (SNRIs) are commonly prescribed as the first line-treatment of depression because they are safer and have fewer side effects than other medications antid. Among SNRIs, duloxetine has shown promise, with multiple experimental studies demonstrating its ability to prevent or alleviate chemotherapy-induced peripheral neuropathy (CIPN). However, SSRI/SNRIs use raise several biological and pharmacological considerations due to clinically relevant drug-drug interactions. Despite the widespread use of antidepressants in this population, robust clinical evidence supporting their efficacy and safety specifically in HM patients remains limited.ObjectiveThe aim of this review is to evaluate the effects of SSRIs/SNRIs in HM, their impact on CIPN, drug interactions relevant to HM therapy, and clinical outcomes of antidepressant use in this population.MethodsFollowing PRISMA guidelines, a systematic search of several databases (PubMed, Scopus and Web Of Science) covering the period from January 1, 2000, to January 31, 2025, was conducted.ResultsA total of 251 articles were initially identified. Ultimately, 24 articles were eligible for analysis. The data relies solely from in vitro studies indicate that SSRIs and SNRIs may enhance the effectiveness of chemotherapy. Only one clinical study evaluated antidepressant efficacy in HM patients, showing improvement in depressive symptoms with paroxetine. Moreover, duloxetine has an established clinical role in the treatment of painful CIPN. However, the evidence supporting its use for CIPN prevention remains limited to preclinical models and lacks definitive clinical validation. The safety issues include serotonin toxicity, a risk of bleeding related to SSRIs and SNRIs impact on platelet functions and other potential drug-drug interactions.ConclusionsBased on available data, it is not possible to clearly recommend SSRIs and SNRIs for HM patients beyond the registered indications. Clinical studies are needed to confirm anticancer and chemosensitizing effects of SSRIs and SNRIs demonstrated in experimental models of leukemia and lymphoma. Nevertheless, the potential broader therapeutic benefits of duloxetine and related serotonergic agents in CIPN warrant further investigation. Due to the high prevalence of depression in HM patients, more data on safety in this population is warranted.
